The Buzi block is operated by a natural gas production partnership between EMP-Buzi Hydrocarbons Pte, Ltd, a subsidiary of PT Energi Mega Persada Tbk, an Indonesia-based upstream oil and natural gas company, and Empresa Nacional de Hidrocarbonetos (ENH), a Mozambique state-owned company. The partners own 75 and 25 percent of the shares respectively.

a6110.t:
The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, has stated that Nigeria anticipated a decline in global financial aid and is actively working towards bolstering its health system by leveraging domestic resources.
Mr Pate, a professor, made this known in a statement issued on Thursday by his Special Adviser on Media and External Relations, Tashikalmah Hallah.
He highlighted that the decline was expected even before the United States government publicly announced cuts to funding for agencies supporting developing countries.
In spite of the challenges, the minister expressed heartfelt gratitude to the US government for its extensive and generous support over the years, acknowledging the positive impact on Nigeria’s healthcare system.
Mr Pate said for the past two decades, many countries worldwide have benefited from lifesaving interventions, particularly in HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria, due to the generosity of the US government and its people.
“For Nigeria, we sincerely appreciate all the support received,” he said.
“However, it is unwise for any country to rely entirely on another for the health and lives of its population.”
Mr Pate reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to prioritising health, noting that the country had made significant advancements in the healthcare sector.
He emphasised the government’s determination to improve the well-being of citizens, and that the cuts in aid were understandable, given the US government’s current interests.
“Here in Nigeria, we are focused on rebuilding our health system, strengthening domestic resources, and providing services for our citizens,” he said.
“We aim to cooperate with other countries in Africa and globally to enhance biosecurity and health security while fostering private-sector investments.”
Additionally, the minister revealed that Nigeria had approved the ratification of the African Medicines Agency Treaty, which would help Nigeria become part of a larger African market for locally produced medicines.
READ ALSO: SPECIAL REPORT: Poor death registration in Nigeria affects identity system, voters register
He also pointed out that there were investment opportunities in Nigeria’s health sector, inviting American partners to participate.
“We have innovations, tools, systems, and technologies that we can trade. We are open and confident that, as the direction of the US government evolves, Nigeria will continue to welcome genuine partnerships with the US and other countries,” the minister said.
“These partnerships should be focused on advancing humanity while respecting each nation’s interests.”
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that on 24 January, the US administration announced a pause in billions of dollars of foreign aid, affecting nearly all foreign aid programmes, pending a 90-day review.
(NAN)

a6262.t:
Financing of health care remain a core issue in most African countries. They are facing critical constraints in financing their health systems to provide a basic package of cost-effective health care interventions deemed necessary to address their health-related challenges. Ensuring affordable access to health services on a continent where one-third of the population lives on less that $1 per day is a daunting challenge. However, it has been rightly observed that, in Africa, increasing the level of health expenditures and improving their efficiency is literally a life and death situation. Different research works reveals that while Africa accounts for less than 0.9 percent of global health spending, the region carries over 43 percent of global burden of communicable diseases, and 24 percent of global burden of diseases.
One of the lessons of the Ebola epidemic is the need to improve the African countries’ public health services, which have suffered the consequences of decades of neglect. Africa needs to rapidly upgrade those services as well as to improve the capacity of its medical and paramedical workforce. Cesar Chelala, a global health consultant stated that although Africa bears one-quarter of the global burden of disease, it only has 2% of the world’s doctors. Progress has been hindered, particularly in rural areas, because the infrastructure and the health services are inadequate, and there is a widespread lack of trained medical personnel.
Effects of HIV/AIDS
The African continent has been greatly afflicted by the HIV/AIDS pandemic. This pandemic has reversed decades of improvement in life expectancy, educational progress and economic growth. For example, in Lesotho, where life expectancy was 60 years in 1995, life expectancy had plummeted to around 50 years in 2017 due, to a large extent, to the HIV/AIDS epidemic in the country. Although the number of deaths of AIDS-related illnesses has fallen significantly in the last decade, the high cost of treating HIV/AIDS, when coupled with the indirect costs resulting from loss of workers’ productivity, has had a serious negative effect on African economies. HIV/AIDS is estimated to have decreased agricultural output by as much as 20% in several African countries.
Cesar Chelala further noted that there has been a sharp increase in non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as diabetes, cancer and heart and lung diseases. The World Health Organization estimates that NCDs will rise in the region by 27% over the next 10 years, resulting in 28 million additional deaths. Mental health problems have traditionally been neglected by African governments. As a result, most mental health patients remain untreated. This “treatment gap” ranges from 75% in South Africa to more than 90% in Ethiopia and Nigeria.
As Dr. Crick Lund, a Professor of Psychiatry and Mental Health at the University of Cape Town has remarked, “By neglecting mental health, it will be difficult to attain many of the Sustainable Development Goals related to poverty, malaria, gender empowerment and education.” Many diseases affecting both children and adults could be addressed with minimum resources if they are adequately employed. This is the case of diarrhea and respiratory infections, measles, malaria, and malnutrition, which represent the greatest threats to children’s health. Malaria is the leading cause of death among African children under five years old. African women are approximately 175 times more likely to die during childbirth and pregnancy than women in industrialized countries.
Sanjeev Ahluwalia, Advisor, Observer Research Foundation in India argued that health problems are worsened by the lack of health professionals, due in part to the continuing exodus of doctors and nurses to industrialized nations. If health care systems are to be effective, resources must be redirected from curative care in urban settings with high tech equipment to primary and preventive health care.
Consequences of corruption
In addition to problems directly related to the health sector, corruption and illicit financial flows drain critical resources needed to improve people’s health and education. According to Kar and Cartwright-Smith, Africa is estimated to have lost in excess of $1 trillion in illicit financial flows. This amount is roughly equivalent to all of the official development assistance received by Africa during the same timeframe. The widespread practice of bribing government officials by foreign companies must be curtailed through the enforcement of national and international laws dealing with this issue.
Cesar Chelala noted that lack of reliable statistics is a hindrance to improving health systems in Africa. They range from defective systems for civil registration to poor data on maternal and child health indicators, including immunization rates for the most common diseases. A World Bank study showed that half the population of African countries had not been included in a census. Reliable statistics are critical for assessing the magnitude and kind of health problems affecting the population, for determining access to health services, particularly in rural areas, for allocating resources for different programs, for assessing the effectiveness of the interventions and for monitoring different projects.
In the last few years, the emphasis has been placed on economic aid to Africa. African countries, however, need a different kind of aid. According to Cesar Chelala they need their human resources to be trained in their own countries. They need more help in preventing major diseases. They need more education for all age levels and they need better conditions of trade for their products. African countries do not need more monetary aid given irresponsibly, which ends up in the hands of government officials and members of the countries’ elites.
To improve people’s health in Africa, more efforts are needed to increase primary health care, especially in rural areas, accompanied by health promotion, disease prevention and improved education for all ages. For too long, Africa has been a photo-op for movie and music stars, whose patronizing attitudes disregarded the Africans’ capacity for solving their own problems.
As writer Paul Theroux wrote about Bono, “There are probably more annoying things than being hectored about African development by a wealthy Irish rock star in a cowboy hat, but I can’t think of one at the moment.” Africa has a tremendous human potential that, well directed, will help overcome the countries’ difficulties. According to current population trends, Africa is set to have the largest youth population in the world. It is estimated that by 2050, the median age for Africa will be 25 years, compared to 36 for the rest of the world. The role of Africa’s youth in guiding the continent’s progress can be considerable if we appeal to its own capacity, creativity and resilience.

a6330.t:
"Un cessez-le-feu à ce stade ci ne bénéficierait qu'au Hamas", a déclaré mardi à la presse le porte-parole du Conseil de sécurité nationale de la Maison-Blanche, John Kirby, qui a aussi prévenu que la situation allait encore empirer pour les civils. Si Washington s'oppose à un cessez-le-feu complet, des arrêts sporadiques dans les combats afin de faciliter l'acheminement de l'aide à la bande de Gaza doivent être "considérés", a-t-il nuancé. "Nous voulons voir les mesures de protection pour les civils. Or des pauses dans les opérations sont un outil, une tactique, qui peuvent y parvenir pour une période temporaire (...) mais cela n'est pas la même chose qu'un cessez-le-feu", a-t-il ajouté. 
                                 
                                                                                                                                                
                                    Une aide humanitaire "pas assez rapide"
Le président américain Joe Biden a estimé mardi que l'aide humanitaire n'arrivait pas assez vite dans la bande de Gaza, assiégée et pilonnée sans relâche par Israël depuis l'attaque sanglante du Hamas le 7 octobre. L'acheminement n'est "pas assez rapide", a déclaré le président américain, questionné par la presse à la Maison-Blanche sur l'aide humanitaire, qui a commencé à entrer samedi, mais au compte-gouttes, dans ce territoire de 362 km2 où s'entassent 2,4 millions de Palestiniens. Dans ce contexte, le secrétaire général de l'Onu Antonio Guterres a appelé à un "cessez-le-feu humanitaire immédiat" entre Israël et le mouvement islamiste palestinien Hamas. "Pour apaiser cette souffrance immense, faciliter la distribution de l'aide de façon plus sûre, et faciliter la libération des otages, je répète mon appel à un cessez-le-feu humanitaire immédiat", a déclaré au siège de l'Onu M. Guterres, en dénonçant des "violations claires" du droit humanitaire à Gaza. "Monsieur le secrétaire général, dans quel monde vivez vous", a lancé le ministre israélien des Affaires étrangères Eli Cohen avant d'annuler sa rencontre avec Antonio Guterres. "Comment pouvez-vous conclure un accord de cessez-le-feu avec quelqu'un qui a juré de tuer et de détruire votre propre existence", a ajouté Eli Cohen face à cette demande de "cessez-le-feu humanitaire immédiat". Le ministère de la Santé du Hamas affirme que 5 791 personnes ont été tuées depuis le 7 octobre et le début des frappes israéliennes sur la bande de Gaza. Ces bombardements sont une riposte à l'attaque sans précédent menée ce jour-là par le Hamas et qui a fait plus de 1 400 morts, tandis que plus de 200 personnes sont retenues en otage.
a6330.en:
United States: The White House repeats that a ceasefire in Gaza “would only benefit Hamas”
“A ceasefire at this stage would only benefit Hamas,” the spokesman for the White House National Security Council, John Kirby, told the press on Tuesday, also warning that the situation would get even worse for civilians. While Washington opposes a full ceasefire, sporadic pauses in the fighting in order to facilitate the delivery of aid to the Gaza Strip should be “considered,” he qualified. “We want to see protection measures for civilians. Pauses in operations are a tool, a tactic, that can achieve that for a temporary period (...) but that is not the same thing as a ceasefire,” he added.
Humanitarian aid “not fast enough”
US President Joe Biden said on Tuesday that humanitarian aid was not arriving fast enough in the Gaza Strip, which has been besieged and relentlessly pounded by Israel since the bloody Hamas attack of 7 October. The delivery is “not fast enough,” said the American president, questioned by the press at the White House about humanitarian aid, which began to enter on Saturday, but in a trickle, into this territory of 362 sq km where 2.4 million Palestinians are crowded together. In this context, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for an “immediate humanitarian ceasefire” between Israel and the Palestinian Islamist movement Hamas. “To ease this immense suffering, to make the distribution of aid safer and easier, and to facilitate the release of the hostages, I repeat my call for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire,” Mr Guterres said at UN headquarters, while denouncing “clear violations” of humanitarian law in Gaza. “Mr Secretary-General, what world are you living in,” said Israeli Foreign Minister Eli Cohen before cancelling his meeting with Antonio Guterres. “How can you conclude a ceasefire agreement with someone who has sworn to kill and destroy your very existence,” Eli Cohen added in response to this demand for an “immediate humanitarian ceasefire.” Hamas's Health Ministry states that 5,791 people have been killed since 7 October and the start of Israeli strikes on the Gaza Strip. These bombardments are a response to the unprecedented attack carried out that day by Hamas, which left more than 1,400 dead, while more than 200 people are being held hostage.

a6533.t:
Mogadishu, SONNA – May 8, 2025 – The Ministry of Defense of the Federal Government of Somalia today received a consignment of military support equipment from the United States, presented by the U.S. Ambassador to Somalia, Ambassador Richard Riley. The equipment is designated for the Somali National Army (SNA).
The newly received military assets are intended to significantly enhance the skills and operational capabilities of the SNA's elite Danab commando force. This support is expected to play a crucial role in ongoing operations aimed at liberating areas from the Al-Shabaab militant group, referred to as Khawarij, and improving the national army's overall capacity to respond to the country's diverse security challenges.
A statement released by the Ministry of Defense welcomed the timely support, specifically highlighting the equipment handed over to the Danab forces. "The Ministry particularly welcomes the support of the equipment that was handed over today to the Danab Commando Forces, which will significantly enhance their operational skills in combating terrorism, and help increase the capacity of the National Army in responding to the country's security challenges," the statement read.
The United States and Somalia maintain a robust military and security cooperation framework. This partnership is primarily focused on counter-terrorism efforts against Al-Shabaab and bolstering regional security initiatives in the Horn of Africa.

a6701.t:
BLANTYRE-(MaraviPost)-Malawi is emerging as a beacon of hope in Africa’s quest for self-reliant healthcare, showcasing how countries can adapt to dwindling donor support while maintaining crucial health services.
Speaking at the Africa’s Roadmap to Self-Reliant Healthcare webinar, Beatrice Matanje, Chief Executive Officer of the National Aids Commission (NAC), emphasized the need for African nations to look inward and fund their own health priorities.
Matanje highlighted Malawi’s commitment to healthcare, citing the allocation of MK5.1 billion to HIV programming to support commodity co-financing, strengthen laboratory sample transport, and recruit frontline health workers.
“The path ahead is not paved with aid but with audacity. Africa has the talent, resolve, and ingenuity to build health systems that serve our people,” Matanje said.
She stressed the importance of adaptive leadership grounded in evidence, as outlined in the Africa CDC’s New Public Health Order.
Matanje also drew attention to examples of governments taking charge, such as Nigeria’s legislature approving an extra $200 million for vaccines and HIV treatment, and Ghana’s presidential directive to cover USAid funding gaps.
Matanje’s remarks come against the backdrop of the 2001 Abuja Declaration, where African countries committed to allocating at least 15 percent of their budgets to health.
However, two decades later, the average spending remains low, at just 7 to 8 percent, with only a few countries meeting the target.
The World Health Organisation recommends a minimum of $86 (approximately K150,000) per person annually for basic health services, but Malawi currently spends about $16 (approximately K28,000) per person.
Despite these challenges, Malawi’s efforts demonstrate a commitment to self-reliance and sustainable healthcare solutions.

a6948.t:
Entre 2005 et 2023, plus de 347 000 violations graves à l’encontre d’enfants ont été constatées dans plus de 30 zones de conflit.
Une femme palestinienne déplacée se tient avec ses enfants à côté des décombres de bâtiments détruits sur la route principale Salah al-Din dans l’est de la ville de Gaza après avoir été forcée de fuir les opérations militaires israéliennes à Beit Lahia dans le nord de Gaza, en Palestine, le 22 octobre 2024.
« La guerre n’est pas saine pour les enfants et les autres êtres vivants », peut-on lire sur une affiche intitulée « Primer » créée par feu l’artiste Lorraine Schneider pour une exposition au Pratt Institute de New York en 1965. Imprimée en lettres minuscules à l’allure enfantine, les mots sont intercalés entre les feuilles d’un simple tournesol. Cette affiche était une réponse précoce à la guerre du Viêt Nam. « Elle voulait simplement faire quelque chose que personne ne pourrait contester », se souvient Elisa Kleven, la fille cadette de Schneider, dans un article publié au début de cette année. Six décennies plus tard, l’hypothèse de Mme Schneider se trouve toujours vérifiée.
Selon Save the Children, environ 468 millions d’enfants, soit un jeune sur six sur cette planète, vivent dans des zones touchées par des conflits armés. Les attaques avérées contre les enfants ont triplé depuis 2010. L’année dernière, les conflits mondiaux ont tué trois fois plus d’enfants qu’en 2022. « Les meurtres et les blessures de civils sont devenus quotidiens », a déclaré Volker Türk, chef des droits de l’homme de l’ONU, en juin, lorsqu’il a annoncé les chiffres de 2023. « On tire sur les enfants. Des hôpitaux bombardés. De l’artillerie lourde cible des communautés entières. »
Il a fallu quatre décennies pour que le Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies rattrape Schneider. En 2005, cet organe mondial a identifié – et condamné – six violations graves commises à l’encontre des enfants en temps de guerre : le meurtre ou la mutilation ; le recrutement ou l’utilisation par les forces armées et les groupes armés ; les attaques contre les écoles ou les hôpitaux ; le viol ou d’autres actes graves de violence sexuelle ; l’enlèvement et le refus d’autoriser l’accès des organismes humanitaires à ces enfants. Le fait de nommer et de dénoncer a toutefois ses limites. Entre 2005 et 2023, plus de 347 000 violations graves à l’encontre de jeunes ont été constatées dans plus de 30 zones de conflit en Afrique, en Asie, au Moyen-Orient et en Amérique latine, selon l’UNICEF, l’agence des Nations unies pour l’enfance. Le nombre réel est sans aucun doute beaucoup plus élevé.
Les enfants sont particulièrement vulnérables en période de conflit, qu’il s’agisse des dommages extrêmes que les armes explosives causent aux petits corps ou des effets durables des privations aiguës sur les cerveaux en développement. Et une fois soumis à la guerre, ils en portent les cicatrices, physiques et mentales, tout au long de leur vie. Une étude récente menée par des chercheurs italiens a souligné ce que Schneider savait intuitivement, à savoir que « la guerre inflige de graves violations aux droits fondamentaux des enfants ». Le traumatisme complexe de la guerre, ont-ils constaté, « constitue une grave menace pour le développement émotionnel et cognitif des enfants, augmentant le risque de maladies physiques et mentales, de handicaps, de problèmes sociaux et de conséquences intergénérationnelles ».
Malgré ces connaissances, le monde continue de manquer à ses devoirs envers les enfants en période de conflit. Les États-Unis étaient, par exemple, l’un des membres du Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies qui a condamné ces six graves violations des droits de l’enfant en temps de guerre. Pourtant, l’administration Biden a donné son feu vert à des dizaines de milliards de dollars de ventes d’armes à Israël, alors que des munitions américaines ont été utilisées à plusieurs reprises pour attaquer des écoles, qui sont devenues des abris, principalement pour les femmes et les enfants, dans la bande de Gaza. « Qu’on ne s’y trompe pas, les États-Unis soutiennent entièrement, résolument, totalement Israël », a récemment déclaré le président Joe Biden, même si son administration a reconnu la probabilité qu’Israël ait utilisé des armes américaines dans la bande de Gaza en violation du droit international.
Et Gaza n’est qu’une zone de conflit où, en ce moment même, des enfants souffrent énormément. TomDispatch vous propose une visite de l’enfer de cette planète, quelques arrêts dans un monde en guerre pour voir ce que les conflits d’aujourd’hui font aux enfants qui en sont prisonniers.
Gaza
Selon l’UNICEF, la bande de Gaza est l’endroit le plus dangereux au monde pour les enfants. Selon les autorités locales, Israël y a tué environ 17 000 enfants depuis le début de l’actuelle guerre de Gaza, en octobre 2023. Fait presque aussi horrible, environ 26 000 enfants auraient perdu l’un de leurs parents ou les deux. Au moins 19 000 d’entre eux sont désormais orphelins ou n’ont pas de famille d’accueil. Un million d’enfants de Gaza ont également été déplacés depuis octobre 2023.
En outre, Israël commet un « scolasticide », c’est-à-dire la destruction délibérée et systématique du système éducatif palestinien à Gaza, selon un rapport récent du Centre Al Mezan pour les droits de l’homme, un groupe de défense des droits des Palestiniens. Plus de 659 000 enfants n’ont pas été scolarisés depuis le début de la guerre. Selon une nouvelle étude réalisée par l’université de Cambridge, le Centre d’études libanaises et l’Office de secours et de travaux des Nations unies pour les réfugiés de Palestine dans le Proche-Orient, le conflit à Gaza va retarder de plusieurs années l’éducation des enfants et risque de créer une génération de Palestiniens traumatisés à vie.
Même avant la guerre actuelle, on estime que 800 000 enfants de Gaza (soit environ 75 % des enfants de la région) avaient besoin d’un soutien psychosocial et de santé mentale. Aujourd’hui, l’UNICEF estime que plus d’un million d’entre eux (en fait, tous les enfants de la bande de Gaza) ont besoin de ces services. En bref, il n’est plus possible d’être un enfant en bonne santé dans cette région.
Liban
Pendant quatre jours, fin septembre, alors qu’Israël intensifiait sa guerre au Liban, environ 140 000 enfants de ce pays méditerranéen ont été déplacés. Nombre d’entre eux sont arrivés dans les centres d’accueil en montrant des signes de profonde détresse, selon le personnel de Save the Children. « Les enfants nous disent qu’ils ont l’impression que le danger est partout et qu’ils ne sont jamais en sécurité. Chaque bruit fort les fait sursauter », a déclaré Jennifer Moorehead, directrice de Save the Children au Liban. « La vie, les droits et l’avenir de nombreux enfants ont déjà été bouleversés et leur capacité à faire face à cette crise de plus en plus grave s’est érodée.
Toutes les écoles de ce pays ont été fermées, ce qui a affecté chacun des 1,5 million d’enfants. Plus de 890 enfants ont également été blessés par des frappes israéliennes au cours de l’année écoulée, la grande majorité (plus de 690) depuis le 20 août, selon le ministère libanais de la santé publique. Etant donné qu’Israël a récemment étendu ses attaques du sud du pays à la capitale libanaise, Beyrouth, ils seront sans doute rejoints par de trop nombreux autres.
Soudan
Les enfants ont énormément souffert depuis que de violents combats ont éclaté à Khartoum, la capitale du Soudan, en avril 2023 entre les forces armées soudanaises (SAF) et les forces paramilitaires de soutien rapide. Plus de 18 000 personnes auraient été tuées et près de 10 millions ont été forcées de fuir leur foyer depuis le début de la guerre civile. Près de la moitié des Soudanais déplacés sont – oui ! – des enfants, soit plus de 4,6 millions d’entre eux, ce qui fait de ce conflit la plus grande crise de déplacement d’enfants au monde.
.Plus de 16 millions d’enfants soudanais sont également confrontés à de graves pénuries alimentaires. Dans la petite ville de Tawila, dans l’État du Darfour Nord, au moins dix enfants meurent de faim chaque jour, selon un rapport publié le mois dernier par le Guardian. La population de la ville a explosé lorsque des dizaines de milliers de personnes ont fui El Fasher, la capitale assiégée du Darfour-Nord. « Nous pensons que le nombre exact d’enfants mourant de faim est bien plus élevé », a déclaré au Guardian Aisha Hussien Yagoub, responsable de l’autorité sanitaire du gouvernement local de Tawila. « Beaucoup de personnes déplacées d’El Fasher vivent loin de notre clinique et sont incapables de s’y rendre. »
Plus de 10 millions d’enfants soudanais, soit 50 % des enfants du pays, se sont trouvés à moins de cinq kilomètres des lignes de front du conflit à un moment ou à un autre au cours de l’année écoulée. Selon Save the Children, il s’agit du taux d’exposition le plus élevé au monde. En outre, l’année dernière, les violations graves des droits des enfants soudanais ont été multipliées par cinq par rapport à 2022.
Syrie
Plus de trente mille deux cents enfants ont été tués depuis le début de la guerre civile syrienne en 2011, selon le Réseau syrien pour les droits de l’homme. Cinq mille deux cents autres enfants ont disparu de force ou sont en état d’arrestation.
Bien que peu remarquée, la Syrie reste la plus grande crise de réfugiés au monde. Plus de 14 millions de Syriens ont été contraints de quitter leur foyer. On estime que plus de 7,2 millions d’entre eux sont aujourd’hui déplacés à l’intérieur du pays, où neuf personnes sur dix vivent en dessous du seuil de pauvreté. Depuis 2011, toute une génération d’enfants vit sous la menace constante de la violence et de traumatismes émotionnels. C’est la seule vie qu’ils aient jamais connue.
« Les services se sont déjà effondrés après 14 ans de conflit », a déclaré le mois dernier Rasha Muhrez, directrice de la réponse de Save the Children en Syrie. « La crise humanitaire en Syrie atteint un niveau record. Plus des deux tiers de la population syrienne, dont environ 7,5 millions d’enfants, ont besoin d’une aide humanitaire. Près de la moitié des 5,5 millions d’enfants en âge d’être scolarisés (2,4 millions âgés de 5 à 17 ans) ne vont toujours pas à l’école, selon l’UNICEF. Environ 7 000 écoles ont été détruites ou endommagées.
Récemment, Human Rights Watch a tiré la sonnette d’alarme concernant le recrutement d’enfants, « apparemment en vue d’un éventuel transfert vers des groupes armés », par une organisation de jeunes affiliée à l’Administration autonome pour le nord et l’est de la Syrie, dirigée par les Kurdes, et aux Forces démocratiques syriennes dirigées par les Kurdes et soutenues par les États-Unis, sa branche militaire.
Ukraine
Le nombre d’enfants victimes en Ukraine a augmenté de près de 40 % au cours du premier semestre de cette année, ce qui porte à environ 2 200 le nombre total d’enfants tués ou blessés en près de 900 jours de guerre dans ce pays, selon Save the Children. « Cette année, la violence s’est intensifiée avec une nouvelle intensité, les missiles, les drones et les bombes provoquant une augmentation alarmante du nombre d’enfants blessés ou tués dans des explosions en plein jour », a déclaré Stéphane Moissaing, directeur national adjoint de Save the Children en Ukraine. « La souffrance des familles ne s’arrêtera pas tant que des armes explosives seront utilisées dans les villes et villages peuplés d’Ukraine. »
Il y a déjà 2,9 millions d’enfants ukrainiens qui ont besoin d’aide, et la situation risque de s’aggraver dans les mois à venir. Les attaques répétées de la Russie contre les infrastructures du pays pourraient entraîner des coupures d’électricité pouvant aller jusqu’à 18 heures par jour cet hiver, laissant de nombreux enfants ukrainiens dans le froid et sans accès à des services essentiels. « Le manque d’électricité et toutes ses répercussions cet hiver pourraient avoir un impact dévastateur non seulement sur la santé physique des enfants, mais aussi sur leur bien-être mental et leur éducation », a déclaré Munir Mammadzade, le représentant de l’UNICEF en Ukraine. « La vie des enfants est accaparée par des pensées de survie, pas d’enfance. »
L’Ukraine estime également que les autorités russes ont enlevé de force près de 20 000 enfants des territoires occupés depuis l’invasion de février 2022. Une enquête du Financial Times a révélé que des enfants ukrainiens enlevés et emmenés en Russie au début de la guerre ont été proposés à l’adoption sur un site web lié au gouvernement russe. L’un d’entre eux était présenté sous une fausse identité russe. Un autre était présenté sous la forme d’une version russe de son nom ukrainien. L’origine ukrainienne des enfants n’était pas mentionnée.
Afrique de l’Ouest et centrale
Les conflits font rage en République démocratique du Congo (RDC) depuis des décennies. World Vision a qualifié la violence qui y sévit depuis longtemps de « l’une des pires crises de protection de l’enfance au monde ». Un rapport des Nations unies sur les enfants et les conflits armés publié en 2023 fait état de 3 377 violations graves commises à l’encontre d’enfants en RDC. Parmi celles-ci, 46 % impliquaient le recrutement d’enfants (dont certains n’avaient que cinq ans) par des groupes armés.
Les violences et les tensions intercommunautaires en RDC ont entraîné la fermeture de 1 457 écoles rien que cette année, affectant plus de 500 000 enfants. Et malheureusement, ce pays n’est pas une anomalie. En mai, le Bureau de la coordination des affaires humanitaires des Nations unies (OCHA) a indiqué que plus de 5 700 écoles avaient été fermées au Burkina Faso en raison de l’insécurité, privant ainsi plus de 800 000 enfants de leur éducation. Selon le Conseil norvégien pour les réfugiés, à la mi-2024, les conflits avaient entraîné la fermeture de plus de 14 300 écoles dans 24 pays africains. Cela représente une augmentation de 1 100 fermetures par rapport à 2023. Les fermetures de 2024 étaient concentrées en Afrique occidentale et centrale, principalement au Burkina Faso, en RDC, au Cameroun, au Tchad, au Nigeria et au Niger. Elles ont touché environ 2,8 millions d’enfants.
« L’éducation est en état de siège en Afrique de l’Ouest et du Centre. Le ciblage délibéré des écoles et le déni systémique de l’éducation en raison des conflits ne sont rien de moins qu’une catastrophe. Chaque jour où un enfant n’est pas scolarisé est un jour volé à son avenir et à celui de sa communauté », a déclaré Hassane Hamadou, directeur régional du Conseil norvégien pour les réfugiés pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest et l’Afrique centrale. « Nous appelons de toute urgence toutes les parties au conflit à cesser les attaques et l’occupation des écoles et à veiller à ce que l’éducation soit protégée et considérée comme une priorité. »
Pieds d’argile
Cela fait six décennies que Lorraine Schneider a dévoilé au monde son affiche et sa sagesse pleine de bon sens. Elle a eu raison à chaque fois, dans tous les conflits de la planète. Partout où les enfants (sans parler des autres êtres vivants) ont été exposés à la guerre, ils ont souffert. Des enfants ont été tués et mutilés. Ils ont souffert de retards physiques, psychologiques et éducatifs, ainsi que de blessures émotionnelles. Ils ont subi des blessures, des agressions et des privations. Leurs corps ont été déchirés. Leur esprit (l’architecture littérale de leur cerveau) a été déformé par la guerre.
Dans les zones de conflit mentionnées ci-dessus et dans tant d’autres (du Myanmar au Yémen) le monde laisse tomber ses enfants. Ce qu’ils ont perdu ne pourra jamais être « retrouvé ». Les survivants peuvent continuer, mais il n’y a pas de retour en arrière possible.
La mère de Schneider, Eva Art, était une sculptrice autodidacte qui a échappé aux pogroms en Ukraine en rejoignant des parents aux États-Unis alors qu’elle était enfant. Selon sa fille Kleven, elle a perdu le contact avec sa famille pendant la Seconde Guerre mondiale et a découvert plus tard que ses proches avaient été tués et que leur shtetl (petite ville juive) avait été entièrement rasé. Pour surmonter son chagrin, Art a fabriqué des figurines en argile représentant les morts de sa ville natale : un garçon et son chien, une femme âgée qui tricote, une mère qui berce un bébé. Aujourd’hui, près de 100 ans après que la jeune Art a été chassée de chez elle par la violence, des enfants continuent de souffrir de la même manière et de se tourner vers l’argile pour trouver du réconfort.
Israa Al-Qahwaji, coordinatrice de la santé mentale et du soutien psychosocial pour Save the Children à Gaza, a raconté l’histoire d’un jeune garçon qui a survécu à une frappe aérienne qui a entraîné l’amputation d’une de ses mains, tout en tuant son père et en détruisant sa maison. En état de choc et replié sur lui-même, le garçon était incapable de parler de son traumatisme. Cependant, diverses techniques thérapeutiques lui ont permis de commencer à s’ouvrir, selon Al-Qahwaji. L’enfant a commencé à parler des jeux auxquels il ne pouvait plus jouer et de la manière dont la perte de sa main avait modifié ses relations avec ses amis. Lors d’une séance de thérapie, on lui a demandé de mouler un objet en argile pour représenter un souhait. Avec sa main restante, il a soigneusement façonné une maison. Après avoir terminé l’exercice, il s’est tourné vers le conseiller pour lui poser une question qui a bouleversé Al-Qahwaji. « Maintenant », a demandé le garçon, « allez-vous amener mon père et me rendre ma main ? »
*
Nick Turse est directeur de la rédaction de TomDispatch et membre du Nation Institute. Journaliste d’investigation primé, il a écrit pour le New York Times, le Los Angeles Times et The Nation, et collabore à The Intercept. Son dernier livre s’intitule Next Time They’ll Come to Count the Dead : War and Survival in South Sudan (La prochaine fois, ils viendront compter les morts : guerre et survie au Sud-Soudan).
Source : TomDispatch, Nick Turse, 22-10-2024
Traduit par les lecteurs du site Les-Crises
Source: https://www.les-crises.fr/
a6948.en:
Between 2005 and 2023, more than 347,000 grave violations against children were recorded in more than 30 conflict zones.
A displaced Palestinian woman stands with her children next to the rubble of destroyed buildings on the main Salah al-Din road in the east of Gaza City after being forced to flee Israeli military operations in Beit Lahia in northern Gaza, Palestine, on October 22, 2024.
"War is not healthy for children and other living things," reads a poster entitled "Primer" created by the late artist Lorraine Schneider for an exhibition at the Pratt Institute in New York in 1965. Printed in tiny, childlike letters, the words are interspersed among the leaves of a simple sunflower. The poster was an early response to the Vietnam War. "She simply wanted to make something that no one could argue with," recalls Elisa Kleven, Schneider's youngest daughter, in an article published earlier this year. Six decades later, Ms. Schneider's premise still holds true.
According to Save the Children, around 468 million children - one young person in six on this planet - live in areas affected by armed conflict. Verified attacks on children have tripled since 2010. Last year, global conflicts killed three times as many children as in 2022. "The killing and wounding of civilians has become a daily occurrence," said Volker Turk, the UN human rights chief, in June, when he announced the 2023 figures. "Children are being shot. Hospitals bombed. Heavy artillery targets entire communities."
It took four decades for the United Nations Security Council to catch up with Schneider. In 2005, that global body identified - and condemned - six grave violations committed against children in wartime: killing or maiming; recruitment or use by armed forces and armed groups; attacks on schools or hospitals; rape or other grave acts of sexual violence; abduction; and the denial of humanitarian access to these children. Naming and shaming has its limits, however. Between 2005 and 2023, more than 347,000 grave violations against young people were recorded in more than 30 conflict zones in Africa, Asia, the Middle East and Latin America, according to UNICEF, the United Nations children's agency. The real number is undoubtedly much higher.
Children are particularly vulnerable in times of conflict, whether from the extreme damage explosive weapons inflict on small bodies or from the lasting effects of acute deprivation on developing brains. And once subjected to war, they carry its scars, physical and mental, throughout their lives. A recent study by Italian researchers underlined what Schneider knew intuitively, namely that "war inflicts serious violations on children's fundamental rights". The complex trauma of war, they found, "constitutes a serious threat to children's emotional and cognitive development, increasing the risk of physical and mental illness, disability, social problems and intergenerational consequences".
Despite this knowledge, the world continues to fail its children in times of conflict. The United States was, for example, one of the members of the United Nations Security Council that condemned those six grave violations of children's rights in wartime. Yet the Biden administration gave the green light to tens of billions of dollars of arms sales to Israel, while American munitions were repeatedly used to attack schools that had become shelters, mainly for women and children, in the Gaza Strip. "Let there be no mistake, the United States fully, resolutely, totally supports Israel," President Joe Biden said recently, even though his administration has acknowledged the likelihood that Israel used American weapons in the Gaza Strip in violation of international law.
And Gaza is only one conflict zone where, at this very moment, children are suffering enormously. TomDispatch offers you a tour of this planet's hell, a few stops in a world at war to see what today's conflicts are doing to the children trapped in them.
Gaza
According to UNICEF, the Gaza Strip is the most dangerous place in the world for children. According to local authorities, Israel has killed about 17,000 children there since the start of the current Gaza war in October 2023. Almost as horrifying, some 26,000 children are reported to have lost one or both parents. At least 19,000 of them are now orphans or have no foster family. One million children in Gaza have also been displaced since October 2023.
In addition, Israel is committing a "scholasticide", that is, the deliberate and systematic destruction of the Palestinian education system in Gaza, according to a recent report by the Al Mezan Center for Human Rights, a Palestinian rights group. More than 659,000 children have been out of school since the start of the war. According to a new study by the University of Cambridge, the Centre for Lebanese Studies and the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East, the conflict in Gaza will set children's education back by years and risks creating a generation of Palestinians traumatized for life.
Even before the current war, an estimated 800,000 children in Gaza (about 75% of the children in the territory) needed psychosocial and mental health support. Today, UNICEF estimates that more than a million of them (in fact, all the children in the Gaza Strip) need those services. In short, it is no longer possible to be a healthy child in this region.
Lebanon
For four days at the end of September, as Israel escalated its war in Lebanon, some 140,000 children in that Mediterranean country were displaced. Many of them arrived at reception centres showing signs of deep distress, according to Save the Children staff. "Children tell us they feel that danger is everywhere and that they are never safe. Every loud noise makes them jump," said Jennifer Moorehead, Save the Children's director in Lebanon. "The lives, rights and futures of many children have already been upended and their capacity to cope with this increasingly severe crisis has eroded."
All the schools in the country have been closed, affecting every one of its 1.5 million children. More than 890 children have also been injured by Israeli strikes over the past year, the vast majority (more than 690) since August 20, according to Lebanon's Ministry of Public Health. Given that Israel has recently extended its attacks from the south of the country to the Lebanese capital, Beirut, they will no doubt be joined by far too many others.
Sudan
Children have suffered enormously since violent fighting broke out in Khartoum, Sudan's capital, in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. More than 18,000 people are reported to have been killed and nearly 10 million have been forced to flee their homes since the start of the civil war. Nearly half of displaced Sudanese are - yes! - children, more than 4.6 million of them, which makes this conflict the largest child displacement crisis in the world.
More than 16 million Sudanese children also face severe food shortages. In the small town of Tawila, in North Darfur State, at least ten children die of hunger every day, according to a report published last month by the Guardian. The town's population exploded when tens of thousands of people fled El Fasher, the besieged capital of North Darfur. "We believe the exact number of children dying of hunger is far higher," Aisha Hussien Yagoub, head of the Tawila local government health authority, told the Guardian. "Many displaced people from El Fasher live far from our clinic and are unable to get there."
More than 10 million Sudanese children, 50% of the country's children, found themselves within five kilometres of the conflict's front lines at one time or another over the past year. According to Save the Children, this is the highest exposure rate in the world. In addition, last year grave violations of Sudanese children's rights increased fivefold compared with 2022.
Syria
More than thirty thousand two hundred children have been killed since the start of the Syrian civil war in 2011, according to the Syrian Network for Human Rights. Another five thousand two hundred children have been forcibly disappeared or are under arrest.
Though little noticed, Syria remains the world's largest refugee crisis. More than 14 million Syrians have been forced to leave their homes. It is estimated that more than 7.2 million of them are today displaced inside the country, where nine people in ten live below the poverty line. Since 2011, an entire generation of children has lived under the constant threat of violence and of emotional trauma. It is the only life they have ever known.
"Services had already collapsed after 14 years of conflict," said Rasha Muhrez, director of Save the Children's response in Syria, last month. "The humanitarian crisis in Syria is reaching a record level. More than two thirds of the Syrian population, including some 7.5 million children, need humanitarian aid." Nearly half of the 5.5 million school-age children (2.4 million aged 5 to 17) are still not attending school, according to UNICEF. Around 7,000 schools have been destroyed or damaged.
Recently, Human Rights Watch sounded the alarm over the recruitment of children, "apparently with a view to possible transfer to armed groups", by a youth organization affiliated with the Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration for North and East Syria and with the Kurdish-led, US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces, its military branch.
Ukraine
The number of child casualties in Ukraine rose by nearly 40% in the first half of this year, bringing to around 2,200 the total number of children killed or wounded in nearly 900 days of war in that country, according to Save the Children. "This year the violence has intensified with a new intensity, with missiles, drones and bombs causing an alarming increase in the number of children wounded or killed in explosions in broad daylight," said Stephane Moissaing, deputy country director of Save the Children in Ukraine. "The suffering of families will not stop as long as explosive weapons are used in the populated towns and villages of Ukraine."
There are already 2.9 million Ukrainian children who need aid, and the situation risks worsening in the months ahead. Russia's repeated attacks on the country's infrastructure could cause power cuts of up to 18 hours a day this winter, leaving many Ukrainian children in the cold and without access to essential services. "The lack of electricity and all its repercussions this winter could have a devastating impact not only on children's physical health, but also on their mental well-being and their education," said Munir Mammadzade, UNICEF's representative in Ukraine. "Children's lives are taken up with thoughts of survival, not of childhood."
Ukraine also estimates that Russian authorities have forcibly removed nearly 20,000 children from the occupied territories since the February 2022 invasion. A Financial Times investigation revealed that Ukrainian children abducted and taken to Russia early in the war were offered for adoption on a website linked to the Russian government. One of them was presented under a false Russian identity. Another was presented under a Russian version of his Ukrainian name. The children's Ukrainian origin was not mentioned.
West and Central Africa
Conflicts have raged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for decades. World Vision has described the long-running violence there as "one of the worst child protection crises in the world". A United Nations report on children and armed conflict published in 2023 recorded 3,377 grave violations committed against children in the DRC. Of these, 46% involved the recruitment of children (some as young as five) by armed groups.
Violence and intercommunal tensions in the DRC have led to the closure of 1,457 schools this year alone, affecting more than 500,000 children. And sadly, that country is not an anomaly. In May, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that more than 5,700 schools had been closed in Burkina Faso because of insecurity, depriving more than 800,000 children of their education. According to the Norwegian Refugee Council, by mid-2024 conflicts had led to the closure of more than 14,300 schools in 24 African countries. That is an increase of 1,100 closures compared with 2023. The 2024 closures were concentrated in West and Central Africa, mainly in Burkina Faso, the DRC, Cameroon, Chad, Nigeria and Niger. They affected around 2.8 million children.
"Education is under siege in West and Central Africa. The deliberate targeting of schools and the systemic denial of education because of conflicts is nothing less than a catastrophe. Every day that a child is out of school is a day stolen from their future and from that of their community," said Hassane Hamadou, regional director of the Norwegian Refugee Council for West and Central Africa. "We urgently call on all parties to the conflict to cease attacks on and occupation of schools and to ensure that education is protected and treated as a priority."
Feet of clay
It has been six decades since Lorraine Schneider unveiled her poster and its common-sense wisdom to the world. She was right every time, in every conflict on the planet. Wherever children (not to mention other living things) have been exposed to war, they have suffered. Children have been killed and maimed. They have suffered physical, psychological and educational delays, as well as emotional wounds. They have endured injuries, assaults and deprivation. Their bodies have been torn apart. Their minds (the literal architecture of their brains) have been deformed by war.
In the conflict zones mentioned above and in so many others (from Myanmar to Yemen) the world is failing its children. What they have lost can never be "found" again. The survivors can carry on, but there is no going back.
Schneider's mother, Eva Art, was a self-taught sculptor who escaped the pogroms in Ukraine by joining relatives in the United States as a child. According to her daughter Kleven, she lost contact with her family during the Second World War and later discovered that her relatives had been killed and that their shtetl (small Jewish town) had been entirely razed. To overcome her grief, Art made clay figurines representing the dead of her home town: a boy and his dog, an elderly woman knitting, a mother rocking a baby. Today, nearly 100 years after the young Art was driven from her home by violence, children continue to suffer in the same way and to turn to clay for comfort.
Israa Al-Qahwaji, mental health and psychosocial support coordinator for Save the Children in Gaza, told the story of a young boy who survived an air strike that led to the amputation of one of his hands while killing his father and destroying his home. In shock and withdrawn, the boy was unable to talk about his trauma. However, various therapeutic techniques allowed him to begin to open up, according to Al-Qahwaji. The child began to talk about the games he could no longer play and about the way the loss of his hand had changed his relationships with his friends. During one therapy session, he was asked to mould an object out of clay to represent a wish. With his remaining hand, he carefully shaped a house. After finishing the exercise, he turned to the counsellor to ask a question that shook Al-Qahwaji. "Now", the boy asked, "are you going to bring my father and give me back my hand?"
*
Nick Turse is managing editor of TomDispatch and a fellow of the Nation Institute. An award-winning investigative journalist, he has written for the New York Times, the Los Angeles Times and The Nation, and contributes to The Intercept. His latest book is entitled Next Time They'll Come to Count the Dead: War and Survival in South Sudan.
Source: TomDispatch, Nick Turse, 22-10-2024
Translated by the readers of the site Les-Crises

a6980.en:
AMERICAN SANCTIONS AGAINST A SENEGALESE JUDGE AT THE ICC: Will Faye maintain his invitation to Trump to come and play golf in Dakar?

The American administration announced, on 20 August, a new set of sanctions against four magistrates of the International Criminal Court (ICC), for abuse of power in several American and Israeli cases. They are the Canadian judge Kimberly Prost, the French judge Nicolas Guillou, as well as two deputy prosecutors, the Fijian Nazhat Shameem Khan [...]

a7048.t:
Vinodia Janete
Magistrados judiciais e do Ministério Público, em Inhambane, harmonizam procedimentos de reforço a proteção da biodiversidade, nas áreas de conservação. A iniciativa, que reúne o judiciário, visa
refletir sobre os desafios que se colocam no combate aos crimes ambientais e à exploração ilegal de recursos naturais.
O país registou no ano passado, mais de trinta e nove mil e seiscentos crimes cibernéticos relacionados a fraude electrónica. Os dados colocam em alerta a Procuradoria-Geral da República que realiza, durante três dias, uma reflexão sobre a cibercriminalidade. Na abertura do evento, o Ministro das Comunicações e transformação digital disse serem necessárias respostas firmes para este tipo de crime.
Empresa Municipal de Mobilidade e Estacionamentos de Maputo enfrenta dificuldades financeiras para reparar e expandir a rede semafórica da urbe bem como modernizar os terminais rodoviários. O PCA da EMME, Francisco Mabzaia diz que, dos cerca de vinte milhões ideais, a empresa municipal arrecada apenas quatro milhões com o estacionamento rotativo, valor insuficiente para transformar Maputo em cidade de sistemas modernos e inteligentes.
Papa Leão XIV manifesta solidariedade às vítimas dos sismos na Venezuela. O sumo pontífice apela ao reforço da ajuda humanitária internacional às populações afectadas pela tragédia.
Muchenga Futebol Clube, Águias Especiais de Lichinga e Real de Cuamba entraram a ganhar na Fase Final do Campeonato Nacional de Futebol da Segunda Divisão do Niassa. Na jornada inaugural deste fim-de semana, Real de Cuamba derrotou a Universidade Pedagógica do Niassa, por 1 x 0. Muchenga Futebol Clube goleou as Águias Especiais de Marrupa por 5 x 0 e Águias Especiais de Lichinga venceram a JJR Ara Norte.
O Distrito de Moatize, na província de Tete, realizou este fim de semana a Primeira Edição do Festival Cultural Sambo Wathu. O evento reuniu cerca de 400 artistas distribuídos em 15 grupos, entre os quais nove
dedicados à dança Njole e seis à dança Mafue, manifestações tradicionais da etnia nhungue.
Captura indiscriminada de espécies marinhas, uso de artes nocivas a pesca e a resistência ao cumprimento do período de veda estão a acelerar a escassez de pescado na baía de Inhambane. Os pescadores reconhecem a redução cada vez mais acentuada de mariscos e apontam a crescente pressão exercida sobre os ecossistemas costeiros e marinhos.
Moradores do Povoado de Niarro, Bairro de Natikiri, em Nampula denunciam o aumento de ataques de crocodilos que já fizeram dezenas de vítimas mortais. Pedem por isso , a construção de uma ponte, para facilitar a travessia de pessoas e bens.
População do Distrito de Moma, pede ao Governo para que reabilite a estrada que liga o Distrito de Mogovolas , à vila sede daquela região costeira da Província de Nampula,. Os comerciantes cujos negócios ainda sobrevivem, afirmam ser muito complicado continuar com a actividade comercial pois, o percurso de cerca de duzentos quilómetros, chega a durar mais de dez horas de viagem.
Duzentas e quarenta e cinco escolas primárias da província de Maputo vão beneficiar, a partir de Outubro próximo, do programa de alimentação escolar denominado “Nutrir para Aprender”. A iniciativa conta com financiamento do Governo dos Estados Unidos da América, no valor de cerca de 40 milhões de meticais, e visa melhorar a literacia e a nutrição, através da redução da fome em crianças em idade escolar.
a7048.en:
Vinodia Janete

Judicial magistrates and public prosecutors in Inhambane are harmonising procedures to strengthen the protection of biodiversity in conservation areas. The initiative, which brings together the judiciary, aims to reflect on the challenges involved in combating environmental crimes and the illegal exploitation of natural resources.

Last year the country recorded more than thirty-nine thousand six hundred cybercrimes related to electronic fraud. The data has put the Attorney General's Office on alert, and it is holding a three-day reflection on cybercrime. At the opening of the event, the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation said that firm responses are needed to this type of crime.

The Maputo Municipal Mobility and Parking Company is facing financial difficulties in repairing and expanding the city's traffic-light network as well as in modernising the road terminals. The chairman of the board of EMME, Francisco Mabzaia, says that of the roughly twenty million that would be ideal, the municipal company collects only four million from rotating parking, an amount insufficient to transform Maputo into a city of modern and intelligent systems.

Pope Leo XIV expresses solidarity with the victims of the earthquakes in Venezuela. The pontiff appeals for the strengthening of international humanitarian aid to the populations affected by the tragedy.

Muchenga Futebol Clube, Aguias Especiais de Lichinga and Real de Cuamba began with wins in the Final Phase of the Niassa Second Division National Football Championship. On the opening matchday this weekend, Real de Cuamba beat Universidade Pedagogica do Niassa 1-0. Muchenga Futebol Clube thrashed Aguias Especiais de Marrupa 5-0 and Aguias Especiais de Lichinga beat JJR Ara Norte.

Moatize District, in Tete province, held the first edition of the Sambo Wathu Cultural Festival this weekend. The event brought together about 400 artists in 15 groups, including nine dedicated to the Njole dance and six to the Mafue dance, traditional expressions of the Nhungue ethnic group.

Indiscriminate capture of marine species, the use of harmful fishing gear and resistance to observing the closed season are accelerating the scarcity of fish in Inhambane Bay. Fishermen acknowledge the increasingly sharp reduction in seafood and point to the growing pressure exerted on coastal and marine ecosystems.

Residents of the village of Niarro, Natikiri neighbourhood, in Nampula, report an increase in crocodile attacks that have already claimed dozens of lives. They are therefore asking for the construction of a bridge to make it easier for people and goods to cross.

The population of Moma District is asking the Government to rehabilitate the road linking Mogovolas District to the main town of that coastal region of Nampula Province. Traders whose businesses still survive say it is very complicated to continue commercial activity because the journey of about two hundred kilometres can take more than ten hours.

Two hundred and forty-five primary schools in Maputo province will benefit, from next October, from the school feeding programme called "Nourish to Learn". The initiative is financed by the Government of the United States of America, to the value of about 40 million meticais, and aims to improve literacy and nutrition by reducing hunger among school-age children.

a7115.t:
The Ombetja Yehinga Organisation (OYO) has reduced its social outreach projects due to USAID funding cuts implemented by the US government earlier this year.
OYO, a non-governmental organisation, focuses on youth education and development through art and works with subcontracted institutions that are USAID-funded.
When the funding was abruptly suspended, the impact was felt immediately.
"When the funding from those partners was suspended, it obviously affected us because we are sub-recipients and rely on that money. So it did affect us. And unfortunately, this year, we could only do fewer projects than we normally do. And we could reach many fewer regions than we normally do," said OYO Director Philippe Talavera.
The organisation, which relies on donor funding, had to find ways to stay afloat and continue advocating for social change.
Of late, the French Consulate in South Africa and the Franco-Namibia Cultural Centre supported a production that will be showcased at the National Theatre of Namibia.
The play Little Prince in Namibia, which encompasses drama, dancing, and music, is derived from a famous French book called Le Petit Prince, translated as Little Prince.
"So it's important to develop the creative sector. But you can only develop the creative sector if people sort of know what it means. For a lot of people, art is a hobby. It's not a job. So we have to start educating people that the creative sector can actually be a job. But as with any job, be it being a doctor, being an engineer, or being a lawyer, it requires training, it requires experience, and it requires exposure. So I think it's important that we encourage young people to explore those opportunities."
The play will be showcased at NTN on the 14th and 15th of this month, and tickets are available at Web Tickets.

a7116.t:
By Richard Chirombo of The Daily Times of Malawi and Hubei-based reporters of China Daily Zhou Lihua, Liu Kun & Zhang Guorong:
Morning light spread over the experimental fields in Blantyre, morning dew dampened the running shoes, with national flags in the orange orchard contrasting with tender green seedlings.
At 6am on September 28, 2025, the unique ‘African Citrus Mini- Marathon’ kicked off warmly at Bvumbwe Agricultural Research Station under the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), South-South Cooperation (SSC) Malawi Phase II Project.
This event, which was premised on the two countries’ ‘friendship’, is not only a celebration of three major happy events in October—the events being the 76th anniversary of the founding of China, the 80th anniversary of FAO’s establishment and the upcoming launch of the Malawi Marathon—but also a vivid demonstration of China-FAO-Malawi SSC’s commitment towards the promotion of shared ideals.
Such an event measures friendship with every step, pays tribute to cooperation through sports and enables the vision of ‘Better Production, Better Nutrition, Better Environment, and Better Life’ to take root with the running steps, adding a warm touch to the friendship of the three parties.
- Advertisement -
More than 50 Chinese and Malawian technicians and some Chinese compatriots in Malawi wore quick-drying clothes that were sponsored by China Yipao Group. They also hoisted the national flags of China and Malawi, ran five kilometres around the boundary of the 267-hectare experimental field within the agricultural station and, finally, checked in at the first citrus observation orchard of SSC in Malawi.
The participants were divided into the Fruit Tree Group, Vegetable Group, Comprehensive Group and Women’s Group for preliminary competitions, with the top four winners being determined in the final.
The initiator of this special marathon event is Liang Suiquan, a senior agricultural expert from China’s Hubei Province and an elite popular runner in Malawi. It is the citrus seedlings he personally cultivated that brought the ‘orange orchard’ and ‘marathon’ together.
In November 2024, Liang introduced nine new citrus varieties and 90 scions from China, and took the lead in demonstrating the grafting and cultivation of 960 seedlings at Bvumbwe Agricultural Research Station in Thyolo District.
- Advertisement -
- Advertisement -
Last February, these seedlings, carrying technology and hope, were transplanted to the experimental field, becoming the ‘stars’ of Malawi’s first citrus observation orchard under SSC.
In less than a year, the seedlings have grown from tiny 1 centimetre (cm) buds to an average height of 45cm.
Last June, Dr. Eviness Pemphero Nyalugwe, who is the Malawi Government Focal Person for SSC, and Dr. Babagana, the FAO Representative in Malawi, visited and inspected the site and spoke highly of this achievement.
“Advancing the citrus pilot observation [initiative] has laid the foundation for the subsequent introduction of mango and apple varieties,” they noted.
No wonder, Suiquan was equally elated.
“[The] Yichang citrus [fruit] has found a new home in Africa,” Liang pointed out, his sentiments not only a testament to the transfer of technology but also the source of inspiration for the event.
This is not surprising, considering that even the preparation of race equipment is filled with heartfelt care that transcends mountains and oceans.
Last February, Liang initiated a campaign on WeChat Moments, calling on members of his hometown’s Yiling Running Association to donate gear.
Zhang Aihua, president of the association, responded promptly, organising fellow runners to donate and contribute sample clothes from previous races, culminating in the collection of over 200 quick-drying shirts.
These love-filled items travelled thousands of miles to Malawi via two groups of ‘messengers’: On August 18, four doctoral students from China Agricultural University, including Li Yuzhe, brought the first batch of 13 kilogrammes of equipment. They were also in Malawi to provide guidance.
On September 3, when Donasius Pathera, the SSC Project Coordinator, led eight officials from Malawi’s Ministry of Agriculture on a visit to China, he made a special trip to the Yiling National Modern Citrus Industrial Park—which is the hometown of foreign aid expert Liang— and then relayed the remaining supplies back.
Yan Wei, a Chinese national from Fujian who has lived in Blantyre for years, learned about the running celebration and voluntarily sponsored over 60 pairs of slippers and prizes, completing the package of all the ‘gifts’ for the ‘African Citrus Marathon’.
“Thank you to my friends and family for helping me realise my dream. I love marathons and I love Malawi’s citrus orchards even more,” Liang pointed out.
He hopes running can serve as a bridge that deepens the friendship between Chinese and Malawian technicians, as they work together toward meeting the ‘Four Betters’ goal which FAO advances.
Dr. Charles Malidadi, who is the SSC Focal Person at the Ministry of Agriculture’s research station, who joined the run, wiped his sweat and smiled excitedly: ‘This is the first time I’ve run on the experimental field with Chinese friends who taught us citrus-grafting techniques. Every step feels like stepping to the rhythm of cooperation.”
From citrus branches in Yiling to citrus orchards in Africa, the ‘Citrus Marathon’—initiated by Liang, with citrus seedlings as the medium and running as the bridge—has weaved agricultural technology exchange and cross-border mutual assistance into every step of the journey. It stands as a vivid reflection of SSC and the deepening bond between the peoples of China and Malawi.
In the morning light of Blantyre, the experimental field-turned-track bears witness to joint efforts; the quick-drying shirts carry concerns from thousands of miles away; and the growing citrus seedlings recording the tangible results of cooperation each passing day and night.
This “small, yet beautiful, initiative”—as Liang puts it— has transformed cooperation from a concept into the sound of side-by-side footsteps, the rustle of growing seedlings and the resonance of connecting hearts.
As more such “small events” come together, the tree of China- Malawi friendship will surely continue to grow toward the sun, nurtured by practical actions and sincere intentions.

a7302.t:
Cassell Anthony Kuoh, the founder and Chief Executive Officer of Liberian 1st Division football club, FC Fassell, has covered the medical expenses of senior female professionals, whose players were hospitalized recently at the ELWA Hospital in Paynesville.
Records reveal that Kuoh, who is also the CEO of New Electric Energy Vehicle (NEEV) Liberia, paid more than US$7,985 for medical bills and transportation costs for the team returning from Guinea.
Earlier this year, the Liberian Upper Women's League club faced a tragic situation following a road accident while traveling to Monrovia from a pre-season camp in Guinea. Goalkeeper Lorpu Forkap and several team members sustained injuries, requiring a 51-day hospital stay.
Speaking via phone Tuesday, October 1, 2024 with journalists, Kuoh said clearing the bills was his way of ensuring the players are fully treated.
Kuoh expressed his commitment to ensuring the players receive appropriate care, stating his hope for their full recovery ahead of the upcoming season.
"It is my prayer that all the players including Lorpu Forkap get back to full fitness for the new season" he said.
Senior Pro President Emmett Glassco extended gratitude to Kuoh for his generous support, highlighting his positive impact on football development nationwide.
“We are very grateful to Kuoh for clearing the bills,” Glassco said.
He described the FC Fassell bank roller, who is a Liberia Football Association (LFA) 2026 Presidential aspirant, as a man with a developmental heart for football across the country.
"What Mr. Kuoh did, only a man with a good heart can do such for a club he has no link with" he explained.
Acknowledging the unexpected assistance from Kuoh, Lorpu Forkah conveyed her appreciation for his financial backing and expressed her determination to return to the field soon, supported by well-wishes from teammates and the sports community.
Forkpah, who was recently released from her sick bed, told journalists that she is indeed grateful for standing with the club financially.
She also hopes to be back on her feet very soon and strong, amidst prayer from members and the sporting community
